prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the freezing and reduced arm swing to Parkinson's disease: the parkinsonism is lower-body predominant, without rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, and improves after CSF removal
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 32% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI (Evans index 0.37, callosal angle 76 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery, given three falls

avoided_actions.rationale: He has no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot help separate iNPH from its mimics.
His falls are trips during freezing, with no syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
He already had a CT; MRI measures the callosal angle, temporal horns and aqueduct better and is available.
The falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; with no rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, a dopamine transporter scan would not change it
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in an 18-month afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is only Fazekas 1, far less than the ventriculomegaly, and the gait improves after the tap.
Freezing and reduced arm swing overlap, but there is no rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia, the nigral hyperintensity is preserved on SWI, and freezing disappears after the tap.
Recall improves with cues within a dysexecutive profile, the hippocampi are MTA 1, and gait led the syndrome.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles are enlarged out of proportion to the sulci, with DESH and a callosal angle of 76 degrees, and the gait improves after the tap.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy as the cause of the gait disorder
differential.key_features: Only mild vibration loss at the great toes with preserved reflexes and proprioception, which does not produce a magnetic gait with freezing.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis in the history.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH needs an insidious gait disturbance after age 40 lasting at least 3 to 6 months with cognitive or urinary symptoms, no antecedent cause, ventriculomegaly (Evans index greater than 0.3) not explained by atrophy, and a CSF opening pressure of 5 to 18 mmHg (7 to 24.5 cmH2O) [Relkin_2005].
DESH and an acute callosal angle support the diagnosis; here Evans 0.37, DESH and a callosal angle of 76 degrees [Nakajima_2021].

The tap test removes 30 to 50 mL and repeats the timed gait measures at 2 to 4 and 24 hours [Nakajima_2021]; a 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive threshold, though no guideline sets a single cut-off. Its sensitivity is 26% to 61% and its PPV 73% to 100%, so a single negative tap does not exclude shunt-responsive iNPH [Marmarou_2005].

Freezing and reduced arm swing occur in iNPH as a lower-body parkinsonism; without rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia or asymmetry, and with freezing that resolves after the tap, no levodopa trial is needed.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild distal vibration loss with preserved reflexes and proprioception does not explain a magnetic gait with freezing, which improves after CSF removal.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Symmetric freezing and reduced arm swing without rest tremor, rigidity or limb bradykinesia occur in iNPH as a lower-body-predominant parkinsonism, and the freezing disappears after the tap.
red_herrings.data_point: Reduced arm swing bilaterally and freezing at doorways
red_herrings.intended_effect: The gait disorder is attributed to Parkinson's disease and a dopaminergic trial replaces the iNPH work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old retired factory supervisor with hypertension and well-controlled type 2 diabetes was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait instability, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline over the past 18 months. His wife first noticed he was walking more slowly and with a shuffle about 18 months ago. She thought he looked 'like an old man all of a sudden.' Over the following months he began to freeze when approaching doorways and narrow spaces, and he has had three falls, twice at home and once in a parking lot. He was previously a confident and active man who enjoyed weekend gardening; he now needs help getting up from low chairs and avoids stairs when possible. His wife notes that he has become noticeably forgetful: he forgets conversations from the day before, has difficulty following the news, and becomes frustrated when he cannot recall words. He denies resting tremor, and his wife confirms she has not seen a tremor. Urinary urgency began approximately 12 months ago and has progressed to frank incontinence with two to three accidents per week. A head CT obtained by his internist at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. He was referred by his internist for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary incontinence. He is anxious about the admission but cooperative.
